Lighthouses

Lighthouses guided ships along dangerous coasts for centuries. The Pharos of Alexandria, built in the third century BC, was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and burned an open fire at its top.

In 1822 Augustin Fresnel invented a lens made of concentric glass prisms that bent scattered light into a single powerful horizontal beam. The Fresnel lens let a lighthouse beam be seen more than twenty nautical miles out to sea and was installed in lighthouses worldwide.

Each lighthouse flashes a unique pattern, its characteristic, so that sailors can identify it at night. Keepers once lived at the station, trimming wicks, winding the clockwork that rotated the lens, and polishing the brass. Today almost every lighthouse is automated and monitored remotely.
